holidays.name: Backwards Day
holidays.description: Flip your day on its head. Wear your shirt backwards, eat dessert before dinner, say goodbye when you walk in, and walk backwards (carefully) down the hallway. Classrooms, offices, and families use it as a cue to do everything in reverse.
holidays.origin: Backwards Day is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It has become a favorite for teachers and parents who want a silly excuse to turn routines upside down.
holidays.funFact: Backwards Day lands on the last day of January, so the month ends with everything reversed.

holidays.name: National Hot Chocolate Day
holidays.description: A day to warm up with a mug of cocoa. Add marshmallows, whipped cream, peppermint sticks, or a pinch of chili for extra kick. It's an easy excuse to cozy up at the end of winter's coldest month.
holidays.origin: National Hot Chocolate Day is an unofficial food observance in the United States. It has been marked on January 31 for years as a way to celebrate the winter staple.
holidays.funFact: The Maya and Aztecs drank chocolate as a bitter, frothy, spiced beverage centuries before anyone thought to sweeten it with sugar and serve it hot.

holidays.name: Eat Brussels Sprouts Day
holidays.description: A day for giving the most picked-on vegetable another chance. Roast them until crispy, toss them with bacon or balsamic glaze, or shave them raw into a slaw. Even longtime skeptics may come around.
holidays.origin: Eat Brussels Sprouts Day is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It encourages people to rethink the little cabbage-like veggie.
holidays.funFact: Brussels sprouts are named after Brussels, Belgium, where they were widely grown in the 1500s. They belong to the same plant species as cabbage, kale, and broccoli.
